lead: Attenuation is the loss of light power as it travels through a fibre. It is measured in decibels per kilometre, and it fixes how far a signal can go before a repeater must restore it. The same fibre also works as a sensor: temperature, strain, pressure or rotation change the light, and a detector turns that change into a measurement. This chapter connects loss budgets, the blocks of a fibre-optic link, and a few fibre-sensor examples.
prereq: You need: 5.7 for total internal reflection and fibre structure, 5.8 for single and multimode fibre, and 5.5 for the laser source.

blocks.text: A light pulse loses power for two reasons: the glass absorbs or scatters it, and the fibre bends. The loss is called attenuation. Engineers quote it in decibels per kilometre, dB/km, because decibels turn a large power ratio into a small number. One dB is not a power; it is a ratio.

blocks.where: α is attenuation in dB/km; L is the fibre length in km; P<sub>in</sub> is the input optical power and P<sub>out</sub> is the output optical power, both in the same unit (W or mW).

blocks.text: A loss of 3 dB means half the power is gone. A loss of 10 dB means one tenth remains. Attenuation is positive when P<sub>out</sub> is less than P<sub>in</sub>. The total loss in dB adds along the link, so a 10 km fibre with 0.2 dB/km loses 2 dB.

items: Absorption: impurities such as OH groups and metal ions take energy from the light and turn it into heat.
Rayleigh scattering: tiny density fluctuations in the glass scatter light in all directions. It grows at shorter wavelength, roughly as 1/λ⁴.
Bending loss: a sharp macro-bend or a small micro-bend lets light escape from the core instead of reflecting.

blocks.text: Silica fibre has low-loss windows near 1310 nm and 1550 nm. Typical single-mode values are about 0.35 dB/km at 1310 nm and 0.2 dB/km at 1550 nm. Attenuation sets repeater spacing: the receiver needs a minimum power to detect bits reliably.
A fibre-optic link converts electrical data to light, sends the light through fibre, and converts it back. The figure shows the order of the blocks.

items: Encoder and driver: formats the data and sets the current that drives the source.
Source: an LED or a semiconductor laser. The LED is cheap and spreads light into many modes; the laser gives narrow, coherent light for long single-mode links.
Optical fibre: carries the light by total internal reflection.
Photodetector: a p-i-n photodiode or avalanche photodiode turns light into current.
Amplifier and receiver: amplify the small current, filter it, and decide whether each bit is 0 or 1.

blocks.text: A repeater is a receiver plus a transmitter: it detects the weak, distorted signal, reshapes it, and sends a fresh pulse. An optical amplifier can boost light directly without converting to electricity. Repeater spacing is chosen from the loss budget. If α = 0.25 dB/km and the link can afford 25 dB, the spacing is 100 km, before margin for connectors and ageing.

A fibre sensor uses a fibre to measure a physical quantity. The quantity changes some property of the guided light: intensity, phase, wavelength or polarization. A detector and signal processor compare the light with a reference and output the measurement.

items: Intensity sensor: a microbend or displacement changes how much light leaks out; the received power gives pressure or position.
Fibre Bragg grating: a periodic index pattern reflects one wavelength. Strain or temperature stretches the grating and shifts that wavelength; the shift is the reading.
Interferometric sensor: phase changes between two paths measure acoustic pressure or tiny strain. A Sagnac loop measures rotation.

blocks.text: Fibre sensors are immune to electrical interference because the sensing signal is light. They do not create sparks, so they suit fuel stores and high-voltage areas. They are small and can be placed far from the electronics. Their limits are temperature cross-sensitivity and the cost of the optoelectronic readout.

examples.question: A 2.0 km long optical fibre has an input power of 1.0 mW and an output power of 0.50 mW. Calculate the total loss in dB and the attenuation in dB/km.
steps: Identify the data: P<sub>in</sub> = 1.0 mW, P<sub>out</sub> = 0.50 mW, L = 2.0 km.
Form the power ratio: P<sub>in</sub> / P<sub>out</sub> = 1.0 / 0.50 = 2.0. The ratio is dimensionless.
Divide by the length in km: α = 3.01 dB / 2.0 km = 1.505 dB/km. To two significant figures, α = 1.5 dB/km.
examples.answer: The total loss is 3.01 dB and the attenuation is 1.5 dB/km (about 1.505 dB/km before rounding).
examples.check:
import math
Pin = 1.0
Pout = 0.50
L = 2.0
loss_db = 10 * math.log10(Pin / Pout)
alpha = loss_db / L
print(round(loss_db, 2))
print(round(alpha, 1))

traps: Attenuation uses log<sub>10</sub>, not ln. A natural-log answer is about 2.303 times larger.
Divide the total loss in dB by the length in km. A total loss is not dB/km.
A dB is a ratio, not a power. Do not add dB directly to mW.
Use both powers in the same unit. mW/mW is fine; mW/W is not.
Bending loss and Rayleigh scattering are both losses, but only Rayleigh scattering has a strong wavelength dependence.

quiz.q: Define attenuation of an optical fibre and give its unit.
quiz.a: Attenuation is the optical power loss per unit length, usually in dB/km. It is α = (10/L) log<sub>10</sub>(P<sub>in</sub>/P<sub>out</sub>), with L in km.

quiz.q: Why does Rayleigh scattering become stronger at shorter wavelengths?
quiz.a: Rayleigh scattering comes from density fluctuations smaller than the wavelength. Its coefficient scales roughly as 1/λ⁴, so blue or shorter light scatters more than infrared light.

quiz.q: A 5.0 km fibre has P<sub>in</sub> = 2.0 mW and P<sub>out</sub> = 0.50 mW. Find the total loss in dB and α in dB/km.
quiz.a: P<sub>in</sub>/P<sub>out</sub> = 4.0; log<sub>10</sub>(4.0) = 0.602; loss = 6.02 dB; α = 6.02/5.0 = 1.20 dB/km.

quiz.q: A 40 km link uses fibre with α = 0.25 dB/km. Input power is 1.0 mW. Find the output power in mW, ignoring connectors.
quiz.a: Total loss = 0.25 × 40 = 10 dB. 10 log<sub>10</sub>(P<sub>in</sub>/P<sub>out</sub>) = 10, so P<sub>in</sub>/P<sub>out</sub> = 10. P<sub>out</sub> = 1.0/10 = 0.10 mW.

quiz.q: What does a repeater do in a long fibre link?
quiz.a: It detects the weakened signal, reshapes and retimes it, and transmits a fresh optical pulse, so the next fibre section starts with enough power and low distortion.

quiz.q: Why is a laser preferred over an LED for a long single-mode link?
quiz.a: A laser launches narrow, coherent light that couples well into a small single-mode core and has low chromatic dispersion; an LED spreads into many modes and couples poorly, so it suits short multimode links.

quiz.q: Name three loss mechanisms in an optical fibre.
quiz.a: Absorption by impurities, Rayleigh scattering, and bending loss (macro-bend or micro-bend).

quiz.q: Why are fibre sensors useful near high-voltage equipment?
quiz.a: The sensing signal is light in a dielectric fibre, so there is no electrical path, no electromagnetic pickup, and no spark risk.

beyond: Not for the exam. Long-haul links now use erbium-doped fibre amplifiers and wavelength-division multiplexing, so many wavelengths share one fibre. Optical time-domain reflectometry (OTDR) finds breaks and splice losses from backscattered light. Fibre Bragg gratings and distributed acoustic sensing turn a whole fibre into a sensor array. Search next for erbium-doped fibre amplifier, OTDR trace, fibre Bragg grating, and Sagnac interferometer.
